title: Fluorescent Nanoparticles for the Measurement of Ion Concentration in Biological Systems
protocol: Aliquot 50 mg Sodium Ionophore X (NaIX) into 1 ml of tetrahydrofuran (THF).
Mix thoroughly in a chemical fume hood to dissolve NaIX completely.
Transfer 100 μl of the dissolved NaIX solution into 10 separate centrifuge tubes.
Repeat the process for sodium tetrakis[3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]borate (NaTFPB).
Allow THF to evaporate overnight in a chemical fume hood.
Label and store the dried NaIX and NaTFPB aliquots at 4°C in a refrigerator.
Dissolve Chromoionophore III (CHIII) in 1 ml of THF.
Add another 1 ml of THF to the CHIII shipping vial to dissolve any remaining CHIII.
Combine both CHIII solutions in a 3 ml glass vial for a total volume of 2 ml.
Transfer 1 ml of the CHIII solution into two separate 1.5 ml glass vials with Teflon caps.
Store the CHIII solution at 4°C in a refrigerator at a final concentration of 5 mg/ml.
Pipette 66 μl of bis(2-ethylhexyl)sebacate (DOS) into a 1.5 ml glass vial with a Teflon coated screw cap.
Weigh out 30 mg of high molecular weight poly(vinyl) chloride (PVC) and transfer this to the optode vial.
Transfer 100 μl of the 5 mg/ml CHIII in THF solution to the optode vial.
Dissolve 5 mg of NaIX in 300 μl of THF.
Transfer 300 μl of the dissolved NaIX solution to the optode vial.
Dissolve a 5 mg aliquot of NaTFPB in 500 μl THF and transfer 20 μl to the optode vial (corresponding to 0.1 mg of NaTFPB).
Add 80 μl of THF to the optode vial.
Mix 30 mg PVC, 60 mg DOS, 5 mg NaIX, 0.2 mg NaTFPB, and 0.5 mg CHIII in 500 μl THF in the optode vial.
Gently vortex the optode vial until all PVC has dissolved.
Allow remaining THF in NaIX and NaTFPB aliquots to evaporate overnight.
Pipette 100 μl of 10 mg/ml PEG-lipid in chloroform into a glass vial.
Evaporate chloroform from the vial in a chemical fume hood or with nitrogen gas/house air.
Add 4 ml of aqueous solution to the vial containing dried PEG-lipid.
Place the vial on a laboratory jack under sonication tip, raising it until tip is about 7 mm deep in solution.
Sonicate at low power (15% amplitude, ½ inch tip diameter step horn) for 30 seconds.
While the solution is being sonicated, mix 50 μl of optode material with 50 μl of dichloromethane in a microcentrifuge tube using a pipette for even mixing.
Adjust the sonifier control to sonicate for 3 minutes.
Add the optode mixture solution to the vial by immersing the pipette tip into the solution and dispensing 100 μl in one quick, even injection.
Allow the sonication to continue for about 30 seconds then lower the jack so that the sonicating tip is about 2 mm deep in the solution.
Pull up the nanosensor solution into a 5 ml syringe.
Attach a 0.2 μm syringe filter and dispense the nanosensor solution into a glass vial with screw top cap.
Make stock solutions of 10 mM HEPES (0 Na) and 1M sodium chloride (NaCl).
pH each of these solutions to 7.2 using trizma base.
Mix stock solutions of 0 Na and 1 M Na in 50 ml conical centrifuge tubes to create solutions with: 0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 mM NaCl concentrations.
Add 100 μl of each concentration of sodium to 3 wells in a column.
Use an optical bottom 96 well plate to determine the response.
Load the plate into a microplate fluorometer.
Read each well with excitation/emission wavelengths of 488 nm/570 nm and 488 nm/670 nm.
Convert either the ratio of intensity at 570 nm divided by the intensity at 670 nm or the intensity at 680 nm to α.
Use plotting software to plot α versus the log of the sodium concentration, setting the log of zero sodium concentration to -1.
Fit a sigmoidal curve to the response.
Calculate the sodium concentration at α = 0.5 from the curve.
Adjust the ratio of CHIII, NaIX, and NaTFPB in the optode to create nanosensors with optimal response around the sodium concentration of interest.
Grow or transfer cells to a glass bottom dish or an imaging chamber with a glass coverslip bottom.
Incubate the cells in clear media or Tyrode's solution.
Mount the imaging chamber or dish onto an epifluorescence microscope.
Pull capillary glass with a pipette puller.
Backfill the pipette with nanosensor solution using a syringe and a Hamilton needle, or a microtip loader and a pipette.
Mount the pipette into a holder that is attached to a micromanipulator and connected to a pressure controlled injection system.
Lower the pipette on top of the cell and into the cytoplasm.
Tap the manipulator holder if necessary to pierce the membrane.
Inject the nanosensor solution.
Withdraw the pipette quickly.
Disinfect the induction and imaging chambers.
Place CD1 nude mice in the induction chamber.
Expose the mice to isoflurane.
Wait for the mice to become fully anesthetized.
Remove the mice from the induction chamber.
Place the mice into the imaging chamber.
Keep the mice under anesthesia.
Disinfect the desired injection areas on the mouse.
Fill a sterile 31G insulin syringe with 10 μL of nanosensors.
Ensure all air bubbles are removed from the syringe.
Using forceps, grasp a small fold of skin along the back of the mouse at the desired injection site.
While grasping the skin, insert the syringe into the skin with the bevel facing up and the needle parallel to the skin.
Prior to injecting the sensors, pull back on the syringe plunger to ensure the needle is not inserted into a blood vessel.
Gently move the needle right and left to create a pocket within the skin.
Inject the sensors and gently remove the syringe.
Gently apply pressure to the injection site and wipe away any solution that may have leaked out of the injection site.
Repeat steps 5.4 through 5.7 until the number of desired injection areas is reached.
For each individual mouse, change needles if the needle becomes difficult to insert into the skin.
Do not share needles between mice to minimize disease transmission or cross-contamination.
Acquire both brightfield and fluorescent images of the mice using filter sets that most closely matched the 640 nm/680 nm (excitation/emission) spectrum of the nanosensors.
